passage: Okay, so for my first month I kept a private list of who sat next to whom in the weekly meeting, Ritu. I am Kalyani, and I thought the sales head had a favourite because the same colleague always sat at his right hand. I also noticed the new hire always chose the end chair, and I decided he was shy or afraid. I nearly told a friend that story. Then I learned the right-hand chair was closest to the projector cable, and the end seat had the only working socket. Habit and logistics, not rank. I stopped guessing. If seating does mean something, it will show in how people are actually treated over time.

qa.q: Why did the same colleague sit at the sales head's right hand?
qa.a: That chair was closest to the projector cable.

qa.q: What did Kalyani first think about the seats, and what changed that view?
qa.a: Kalyani first thought the seating showed favouritism and fear, but learned it was logistics like the cable and the socket. Seating can reflect rank, but here the evidence pointed elsewhere.

qa.q: What would you advise Kalyani about reading seating in the future?
qa.a: Kalyani can look at how people are treated over time and check facts before guessing at hidden meaning.

qa.q: How might the new hire have felt about Kalyani's private list?
qa.a: The new hire may have been unaware, and would probably feel misjudged if told the end chair meant fear when it was about the socket.

grounding: Spoken monologue on a young professional reading seating and distance in meetings, learning it can be habit or logistics.

passage: I sit near Nirmala in the office in Dharamshala and I notice things. On Monday, Tenzin, the new manager, took the chair at the long table's corner instead of the head, and Nirmala took the seat farthest from him. Two colleagues made a show of sitting close beside Tenzin. I could not tell whether anyone meant anything by it. Later Nirmala said the far chair had the only window and the only fan. Tenzin, when I asked lightly, said the corner chair was where the light was best for reading. I think I was wrong to read a story into it at first. People's positions can be rank, comfort or just where the fan is.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin sit at the long table?
qa.a: Tenzin took the chair at the corner.

qa.q: What might the narrator have been thinking about the seating at first, and what changed that?
qa.a: The narrator suspected the seats showed rank and distance, but learned Nirmala's chair had the only window and fan, and Tenzin's had the best light. The seating was about comfort.

qa.q: What could the narrator do next time before guessing at meaning?
qa.a: The narrator could ask lightly, as was done with Tenzin, or watch how people behave over time.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt about being seen as distant?
qa.a: Nirmala may have been surprised, since the seat was chosen for the window and fan and not for distance.

grounding: Observer's account of a young professional reading seating in a meeting as status, learning it can be habit or logistics.

passage:
Monday: At the weekly review, Sangeeta took the chair right next to Mr. Dutta again. Third week running. Trisha, at the far end of the table, felt a small prickle. Teacher's pet, she thought.
Wednesday: When Mr. Dutta praised Sangeeta's report, the prickle turned sour. Trisha told a friend at lunch, "Sit beside the boss and your work gets noticed. Wonderful system."
The following Monday: Trisha arrived early and, on impulse, took the chair next to Mr. Dutta herself. Sangeeta came in with her laptop, paused, and said pleasantly, "Oh, could we swap? I take the minutes, and I need to see his screen to copy the action points. It's a pain from the far end." Trisha went red. "Of course." Walking back to her usual spot, she thought about her lunch comment and felt worse.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta need to sit next to Mr. Dutta?
qa.a: She takes the minutes and needs to see his screen to copy the action points.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: Trisha felt resentful and a little jealous, assuming Sangeeta's seat near the boss was why her work got noticed.

qa.q: What could Trisha have done instead of assuming?
qa.a: Looked for other reasons or simply asked, since the seat turned out to be about taking minutes, not about being a favourite.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel if she heard about Trisha's lunch comment?
qa.a: Sangeeta might feel hurt and misjudged, since she sits there for a practical reason and earned the praise for her report.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading meeting seating as favouritism when it was logistics, and how the assumption led to misjudgment.

passage: Farhan, you're wondering why the quiet fellow always sits beside your boss at lunch. Let me, Yusuf, tell you about Mr. Pinto. I was twenty-four, a junior clerk at a shipping office near the docks. Pinto sat at the desk right outside the manager's cabin, and whenever someone came late, the manager seemed to know. So I decided Pinto was the manager's spy. I avoided him for a whole year, kept my voice down near his desk, told the other juniors to be careful. Then one monsoon the roof leaked and we all had to shift. Pinto moved without complaint to the far corner. And the manager still knew who came late, because he checked the attendance register every morning. Pinto had sat there for nineteen years simply because it was his first desk. He was also the kindest man in that office. I had wasted a year.

qa.q: How many years had Mr. Pinto sat at that desk?
qa.a: Nineteen years.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel about Mr. Pinto during that first year?
qa.a: Yusuf felt suspicious and wary, sure Pinto was the manager's spy, and kept away from him.

qa.q: What turning point showed Yusuf the truth about the seating?
qa.a: When the roof leaked and Pinto moved to the far corner, the manager still knew about latecomers from the attendance register, so the seat meant nothing.

qa.q: How might Mr. Pinto have experienced that year of Yusuf avoiding him?
qa.a: He may have felt puzzled or a little lonely, treated warily by a junior for no reason he knew of.

grounding: An elder recalls reading a colleague's seat near the boss as spying when it was only habit, and the misjudgment it caused.

passage: The offsite had been moved at the last minute to a cramped room above a Chandigarh restaurant, with eight chairs for eleven people and a smell of frying from the kitchen. The director took the head of the table, and the senior leads filled the chairs beside him. Salma, the most senior of them all, stayed standing at the back by the door. Gurleen, three months into the job, watched her all morning. Everyone knew Salma had argued against the reorganisation. Was this a protest? A way of saying "not my plan"? At the tea break Gurleen almost repeated the theory to a colleague, then stopped herself and went over to Salma instead. "Would you like my chair? I'm happy to stand." Salma smiled. "Kind of you, but no. My mother's in hospital, and I may need to step out for calls. By the door is easier."

qa.q: How many chairs were there for how many people?
qa.a: Eight chairs for eleven people.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as Salma stood at the back?
qa.a: Gurleen felt curious and a little uneasy, wondering whether Salma was protesting against the reorganisation she had argued against.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do instead of spreading her theory?
qa.a: She stopped herself and offered Salma her chair, which opened a kind conversation and revealed the practical reason.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt if people assumed she was protesting?
qa.a: Salma might have felt misjudged and more stressed, already worried about her mother and standing by the door only for calls.

grounding: Shows a young professional tempted to read a senior's position in a meeting as protest, and a kind question revealing a practical reason.

passage:
In the Hyderabad office's weekly review, Sangeeta noticed the same pattern three Mondays running: Trisha always took the chair right next to the director, close enough to see his notes. Two senior managers sat at the far end, near the door.
By the third week Sangeeta had built a whole theory. Trisha was the favourite. The seniors were out of favour. She had better sit closer too.
On the fourth Monday she arrived early and took the chair beside the director's. Trisha came in with a laptop and a tangle of cables, stopped, and smiled awkwardly. "Oh. Would you mind? I run the projector and take the minutes, and the cable only reaches here."
Sangeeta's ears burned. She moved. Later she asked one of the seniors why they sat by the door. "Back-to-back calls," he said. "We slip out at eleven."
Nothing hidden. Just cables and calendars.

qa.q: Why does Trisha sit next to the director?
qa.a: She runs the projector and takes the minutes, and the cable only reaches there.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Trisha explained about the cable?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt embarrassed, ears burning, seeing that the theory about favourites had no real evidence behind it.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta have done before building a theory?
qa.a: Asked someone casually why people sat where they did, or waited for real evidence, instead of reading rank into the seating. 🙂

qa.q: How did Trisha seem to feel finding her chair taken?
qa.a: Trisha seemed awkward and a little flustered, since she needed that spot for her work and had to ask for it.

grounding: Seating near the boss can come from logistics or habit rather than rank, and assuming a hidden meaning without evidence leads to misjudgment.
